name: Azaziah
title: Levite and overseer of temple offerings under King Hezekiah
summary:
Asaiah was a Levite who served under King Hezekiah of Judah at the end of the 700s BC.  
He was appointed as one of the overseers responsible for managing the people's voluntary offerings, tithes, and holy contributions in the temple in Jerusalem.  
The appointment took place as part of Hezekiah's extensive religious reform, during which temple service was restored and thoroughly reorganized after a period of decline.  
Asaiah served under the leadership of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, and was one of ten named overseers who ensured fair collection and distribution of gifts to priests and Levites.  
His service testifies to the central role the Levites played in the administration of the temple, and to Hezekiah's desire to reestablish a reliable and orderly management of the sanctuary.

The appointment took place as part of King Hezekiah's religious reform, during which the temple operations and the Levites' service were systematically reorganized.

versions.summary: Azaziah (Hebrew: Azayahu) is a name that appears several times in the Old Testament, referring to various individuals in the history of Israel and Judah. The most well-known Azaziah was a Levite who served under King Hezekiah and was involved in the temple reform. The name means 'the Lord has done' or 'the Lord has acted'.
versions.title: Levite and temple servant
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Levite and temple servant' is reasonable, but the profile mixes several different people named Asaiah. It should either be clarified that this is a composite profile or focus on one specific person. If the focus is the Levite under Hezekiah, the title is fine, but 'leader' under roles is then somewhat imprecise.; [major] The role 'priest' is imprecise. Asaiah in 2 Chr 31:13 is described as a Levite and overseer, not as a priest. Levites and priests were different roles in the Old Testament. The role should be changed to 'Levite' and possibly 'overseer'.; [minor] The meaning of the name is given as 'the Lord has done' or 'the Lord has acted'. The Hebrew עֲשָׂיָ֫הוּ (Asajahu) more precisely means 'Yahweh has done/acted', which is correct, but the Hebrew transliteration should be more accurate. The form 'Asajahu' is acceptable.; [minor] The summary mixes several people named Asaiah. It should be clarified which Asaiah the profile primarily concerns, and it should be stated more clearly that other references (such as Neh 11:5 and 1 Chr 6:30) likely concern different people.; [major] In 2 Chr 29:12-14 several Levites are mentioned, but the name Asaiah does not appear explicitly among them in most translations. Other names such as Mahath, Joel, Kish, etc., are mentioned. This reference should be carefully verified, as it may be incorrect.; [minor] The event 'Mentioned in Ezra's genealogy' has the title 'Ezra's genealogy', but the reference is 1 Chr 6:30 (bookId 13), which is Chronicles, not the book of Ezra. Thus, the title and description are misleading.; [minor] The event concerning Neh 11:5 (bookId 16) mentions an Asaiah among Judah's descendants who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. This person is likely a completely different individual from the Levite under Hezekiah and belongs to a different time period (after the exile). Mixing this in without clarifying that it is another person is confusing.; [minor] The events 'Overseer over temple offerings' and 'Service during Hezekiah's spiritual renewal' largely overlap. 2 Chr 31:12-14 and 31:13 refer to the same context. These should be merged into one event to avoid redundancy.; [minor] According to 2 Chr 31:13, Asaiah was under the leadership of Konaniah and Shimei. Furthermore, genealogies in 1 Chr 6 can provide more family information. The father should be investigated further.

versions.summary:
Asaiah (Hebrew: Asayahu, 'Yahweh has acted') was a Levite who served under King Hezekiah of Judah.  
He was among the overseers given responsibility for managing the voluntary offerings, tithes, and sacrifices in the temple during Hezekiah's major religious reform.  
The name Asaiah appears in several places in the Old Testament and may refer to different individuals, including a Levite mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles (1 Chron 6:30) and one of Judah's descendants who settled in Jerusalem after returning from exile (Neh 11:5).  
These are likely different people from different time periods.

versions.summary: Asahiah (Hebrew: Asayahu, 'Yahweh has acted') was a Levite who served under King Hezekiah of Judah in the late 700s BC. He was appointed as one of the overseers responsible for managing the people's voluntary offerings, tithes, and holy contributions in the temple at Jerusalem. This appointment took place as part of Hezekiah's extensive religious reform, during which temple service was restored and systematized. Asahiah served under the leadership of Konaniah and his brother Shimei, and was one of ten named overseers tasked with ensuring the fair collection and distribution of gifts to priests and Levites. His service testifies to the important role Levites played in the administration of the temple, as well as Hezekiah's desire to organize temple operations in a reliable and transparent manner. The name Asahiah also appears elsewhere in the Old Testament and may refer to different individuals from other time periods.

A shorter and more concise title would make the profile more readable.; [minor] The transliteration and Hebrew forms in the first footnote should be double-checked. The form עֲשָׂיָה is usually transliterated as 'Asajah', while 2 Chr 31:13 in the Hebrew text has the form עֲזַזְיָ֡הוּ (Azazjahu). It is important to distinguish between the names Asajah and Azazjah, which may represent two different Hebrew names.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew name rendered as 'Azaziah' in 2 Chron 31:13 is עֲזַזְיָ֫הוּ (Azazjahu), composed of the root עזז ('to be strong') and the divine name Yahweh (-jahu). The name thus likely means 'Yahweh is strong' or 'Yahweh has strengthened'. It is a theophoric name reflecting the widespread practice in Israel and Judah of including the divine name in personal names.

King Hezekiah's temple reform (c. 715–686 BC) was one of the most comprehensive religious reforms in Judah's history. According to the Books of Chronicles, it involved cleansing the temple, restoring sacrificial worship, and systematically organizing the Levites' service, including the management of tithes and offerings.

The distinction between priests (descendants of Aaron) and Levites (other members of the tribe of Levi) was fundamental to the Israelite temple system. The Levites had various duties such as singers, gatekeepers, and overseers, but did not perform the sacrificial service itself, which was reserved for the priests.

In 2 Chron 31:13, Azariah is mentioned among ten named overseers who served under Konaniah and his brother Shimei. This administrative structure with named responsible persons testifies to a well-organized temple economy during Hezekiah's reign.

Archaeological finds of royal seals and bullae from the time of Hezekiah – including seals with the inscription 'Belonging to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah' – confirm that the king had a well-developed administrative apparatus. Although no seal is directly linked to Azariah, the findings support the picture drawn by Chronicles of an organized administration.

The list of overseers in 2 Chron 31:13 is a rare example of a detailed administrative document preserved in the biblical text. Such lists with named officials suggest that the author had access to official archives or temple records from Hezekiah's time.
